Brown Act
Agendas are drafted to accurately state what the legislative body is being asked to consider.
The legislative body can take action on "all items" listed on the agenda and be in compliance
with the open meeting laws. Under the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless
it is listed on the agenda, or unless certain emergency or special circumstances exist. The
governing body may direct staff to investigate and/or schedule certain matters for
consideration at a future meeting.

   Parks & Recreation Commission Regular Meeting
  August 13, 2026
  STAFF REPORT ITEM No. 1
To:  Honorable Parks & Recreation Commission
From:  Tina De La Rosa, Director of Parks & Recreation
Date:  July 26, 2026

Subject:  Review of Recreation Programs 4th Quarter FY 2025/26

Recommended Motion:  Motion to receive and file.

Report Summary:

Aquatics
The fourth quarter marked the start of the Swim Stadium’s busiest season, bringing increased
participation across many of our aquatic programs despite continued staffing challenges. Even
with these obstacles, the Aquatics Division successfully expanded program offerings, welcomed
more participants, and continued providing quality instruction and community events.

Our Learn-to-Swim program experienced strong enrollment throughout the quarter, serving a
total of 2,054 participants. Group swim lessons accounted for 1,476 enrollments, while 247
individuals participated in private lessons and 331 enrolled in semi-private instruction.
Participation remained strong across all age groups, including 200 Parent & Child participants
(ages 6 months–2 years), 642 Tiny Tots (ages 3–5), 1,122 Youth (ages 6–17), and 90 Adults
(18 and older). Seasonal programming also continued to grow, with Splash Camp already
reaching 92 participants and continuing to enroll throughout the summer. Additional specialty
offerings included a Swim Clinic with 10 participants and the launch of a new Teen Program,
which attracted 18 participants and continues to gain momentum.

The quarter also featured several successful community events that promoted water safety and
encouraged residents to enjoy the Swim Stadium. Our annual Easter Splash Fest welcomed
approximately 240 participants for a day of family-friendly activities, while the Water Safety Bash
drew almost 100 attendees in celebration of Water Safety Month. We also participated in the
World's Largest Swimming Lesson, providing water safety education and swim instruction to
almost 50 participants. Two new events debuted this season—the Aquatics Open House and
the Aqua Fitness Expo—which introduced community members to our aquatic programs, fitness
opportunities, and facility amenities while helping generate interest in memberships and future
programming.

The Swim Stadium remained a regional hub for competitive aquatics throughout the quarter.
More than 3 club swim teams and one high school team utilized the facility for practices,
reinforcing the stadium's reputation as a premier training venue. We also hosted five swim
meets, including two high school competitions and three South Central Swim League meets,
  Page 1 of 7

  4
 welcoming hundreds of athletes, coaches, and spectators to the facility.

Five staff training sessions were conducted during the quarter, including annual lifeguard
recertification training that renewed certifications for 30 returning lifeguards. These trainings
helped ensure staff maintained the knowledge and skills necessary to provide a safe and
positive experience for all visitors.

Membership activity continued to trend upward as the summer season began. The introduction
of the new Summer Splash Pass provided residents with an affordable recreational swim option,
while new summer aquatic fitness classes expanded opportunities for adults seeking low-impact
exercise. Private rentals also remained popular as families and organizations continued to
utilize the Swim Stadium for celebrations and special events.

Fitness
Total Fitness memberships sold or renewed during the 4th Quarter increased to approximately
3,000, an increase from the 2,800 recorded in the previous quarter. Premier Memberships
increased from 550 to about 650 active members, while Sports/Splash Memberships currently
total around 450. Sports Center check-ins for the quarter reached approximately 23,500 in the
3rd quarter. Fitness daily admissions totaled around 900, while Sports daily admissions came in
at approximately 3,700. The absence of the Junior Athletic Association’s indoor basketball
season during this period allowed for more open gym availability, contributing to the steady
usage of the facility for recreational play.

The Personal Training program saw a steady number of packages sold this quarter, while total
training hours delivered remained consistent. This trend aligns with seasonal patterns, as
warmer weather typically drives higher interest in fitness services. The Private 12-session
package continued to be the most popular offering, followed by the Private 4-session option.

The Annual Spring Fit 5K took place on May 9, marking the 9th year of the event. Once again
Bimbo was the title sponsor and provided the race shirts. The race welcomed over 1,250
participants and more than 400 spectators. The Spring Fit 5K remains our largest race of the
year, setting the stage for the upcoming Fun Run in July. The vendor fair accompanying the
event was a major highlight, featuring raffle give-a-ways sponsored by Raising Cane’s and
Bimbo, while Northgate Markets provided water bottles and fresh fruit for participants.
Lastly, Fitness staff participated in the Summer Kick-Off event on Wednesday, June 3, from 3-
7pm. The event invited community members to explore Parks and Recreation programs and
services. Fitness hosted an outdoor Step Aerobics session and operated a promotional booth,
alongside other Divisions, as part of the Department’s family-friendly showcase.

Youth Sports
All Youth Fundamental Sports classes offered during the spring session experienced
exceptionally high demand, reaching full enrollment within just a few days of registration
opening. The success of the spring session can largely be attributed to the favorable weather,
which provided ideal conditions for outdoor sports and recreational activities. Attendance
remained strong and consistent throughout the program, and all participants were recognized
with certificates of completion on the final day of class.
During Spring Break (March 30–April 3), coaches hosted a sold-out weeklong Sports Camp
featuring a different sport each day, including soccer, flag football, volleyball, basketball, and
baseball. The camp provided participants with the opportunity to develop new skills while
enjoying a fun, engaging, and active environment. Each participant received a South Gate
Sports Camp T-shirt and a newly designed custom sack pack as part of the program.
Summer registration opened on June 8 and reached full capacity within hours, making it the
  Page 2 of 7

  5
 most popular session of the year. The high demand is largely attributed to participants having
greater availability during summer break. Classes are currently in progress and are scheduled
to conclude on August 20. Throughout the session, the Youth Sports staff have continued to
provide high-quality instruction with a strong emphasis on fundamental skill development, player
growth, and maximizing each participant's performance in a positive and supportive learning
environment.

Adult Sports
The fourth quarter began with the conclusion of the Winter Adult Softball season, which was
extended by approximately three weeks due to inclement weather. The season concluded at the
end of April, with a total of 42 teams competing across seven divisions for their respective
championships.
The Spring 2026 Adult Softball season began in May and is currently underway, with league
play scheduled to conclude at the end of August. A total of 39 teams are competing across
seven divisions for the opportunity to win a league championship. Championship teams will be
recognized with commemorative team sweaters and a championship trophy in recognition of
their accomplishments.
During the fourth quarter, Open Play Volleyball continued to be one of the department's most
well-attended weekly recreation programs, particularly on Tuesday evenings. In response to the
growing popularity of the program, the department will host its second annual Volleyball After
Dark event in August, providing participants with an enhanced recreational experience. Interest
in the program remains strong, with both new and returning players consistently attending
multiple pick-up games each week. South Gate Park continues to be one of the few locations in
the surrounding area to offer organized open play volleyball opportunities.
In preparation for the fall season, staff are actively recruiting participants for the upcoming Men's
and Women's Basketball and Volleyball leagues. Recruitment efforts have generated positive
interest, with the goal of launching all leagues this fall and expanding recreational opportunities
for the community.

Partner Organizations (Sports):
The SG Aztecs hosted monthly recruitment booths throughout the fourth quarter at South Gate
Park to increase program registration and community awareness. In addition to their recruitment
efforts, the organization participated in the annual Spring Fit 5K, with members competing as
event runners and representing the program within the community.
SGJAA hosted its Spring Baseball/Softball Opening Day on May 2. The event featured baseball-
themed music, a team parade across the field, and welcoming remarks from JAA Board
members, who expressed their appreciation for the continued support of the community. The
celebration concluded with complimentary hot dogs, chips, and beverages for all participants
and attendees. The season was extended by several weeks due to issues with the field lighting
but is scheduled to conclude in mid-July. In preparation for the next season, registration for the
Summer Basketball league opened, with team practices beginning shortly thereafter.
AYSO successfully concluded its spring season and is now preparing for its fall season, which is
scheduled to begin in September. Online registration is currently open, and the organization
continues to recruit participants in anticipation of another successful season.

Remote Programming
The fourth quarter was highlighted by the successful launch of several new remote programs
designed to introduce and promote Eastside parks as vibrant community spaces. A key initiative
is the Eco Gardening Workshop held at Urban Orchard Park, which accommodates 40
participants per session and has generated significant community interest. This program is
offered in partnership with the Water Replenishment District and provides a comprehensive

  Page 3 of 7

  6
 three-part series covering edible gardening, pest and weed management, and proper pruning
techniques. Hosting these workshops at one of the newest parks has effectively encouraged
residents to explore and engage with the amenities available at Urban Orchard Park.

In addition, new recreational sports classes have been introduced for youth, including
fundamentals in pickleball, basketball, and futsal. Among these, the futsal program has
emerged as the most popular, focusing on developing quick footwork, ball control, passing,
movement, and teamwork through engaging drills that build both skill and confidence. These
classes are held at Circle Park, a recently developed facility featuring a futsal court, full
basketball court, pickleball court, fitness equipment, and a playground, making it a versatile
destination for families and community members.

For adults, a Mindful Movement Yoga class has been introduced at Hollydale Community Park.
This program focuses on foundational yoga principles, including basic postures, gentle
stretching, breathing techniques, and body awareness, all within a supportive and accessible
environment. The class has been well received, particularly as a weekly Thursday morning
offering, contributing to increased community engagement at the newly remodeled park.

Lastly, the Saturday Steppers Walking Club offers an inclusive, all-ages opportunity for physical
activity while showcasing Eastside parks. This program rotates monthly between locations such
as Urban Orchard Park, Circle Park, Hollydale Community Park, and Hollydale Regional Park.
Participants enjoy one-mile walks at their own pace, promoting health, social interaction, and
greater familiarity with the city’s outdoor spaces. Collectively, these programs demonstrate a
strong commitment to expanding recreational opportunities and fostering community connection
across the Eastside.

Special Events:
Memorial Day was held on Saturday, May 23. This event would not have been possible without
the assistance of our guest speaker Staff Sergeant Abel Vital, Bishop Juan Carlos Mendez,
Lieutenant Carlos Corella, Officer Juan Garcia, and the South Gate Explorers. Attendees were
welcomed with our Memorial Day Program and light refreshments.

Our department proudly hosted our 2nd Annual Summer Kick-Off, held on June 11. This event
was strategically designed to strengthen collaboration among all divisions within the Parks and
Recreation Department while enhancing our engagement with the community we serve. A
highlight of the event was an interactive challenge that encouraged participants to visit every
facility in the park to earn a complimentary food plate. Passport cards were successfully
distributed and completed; also, staff were able to engage patrons in meaningful conversations
as they visited each facility for their stamp. Lastly, each division displayed its services in a
vibrant resource fair, where themed booths lined the open grass area and provided attendees
with exciting new programming opportunities, they had not previously discovered.

Social Media:
Our total followers are now up to 9,522 an increase of nearly 2,000 from the last quarter. In our
Spring quarter we had 17 posts and 135 stories. We have reached over 52,073 accounts and
achieved a profile activity of 9,179. Our Recreation Marketing Coordinator role was vacant
during the last quarter of the fiscal year, but our team rallied together to ensure content was still
created and marketed.

Teen Program:
Friday programs experienced significant growth, with many events drawing more than 20
participants. Highlights included an obstacle course challenge featuring relay-style team
competitions using hula hoops, chalk, puzzles, ping pong, basketball, and other equipment.

  Page 4 of 7

  7
 Teens also enjoyed the popular Smash Bros & S'mores event, where they roasted hot dogs and
s'mores while participating in a friendly Nintendo Switch tournament. Another standout event
was Laser Tag, where 25 teens competed in team matches inside an army-themed arena
complete with strobe lights, music, and fog effects, with raffle prizes awarded to participants.
The largest Friday event was the Last Bell Bash, which celebrated the end of the school year
with water slides, games, and summer kickoff festivities.

Staff also participated in the Legacy High School Wellness Fair, promoting the Teen Center's
summer programs and excursions while engaging students through Minute to Win It games and
a Post-it art activity.

The Teen Center successfully hosted its first fundraiser during the Spring Recitals to help offset
costs for upcoming summer excursions. In addition, the program introduced its first teen field
trip since reopening in September, with a successful Spring Break excursion to Knott's Berry
Farm, marking an exciting milestone for the program's continued growth.

Contract Classes:
Spring classes had a great session, with increased registrations and most classes filling to
capacity. Staff worked closely with instructors to prepare updated class rosters, recital lineups,
parent information letters, and recital tickets to ensure everything was organized for the end-of-
session performances.

The Spring Recitals were a huge success. Tuesday evening's performance sold out, and
families continued to show great support throughout the Wednesday and Thursday
performances. Participants had the opportunity to showcase everything they learned during the
session, making it a rewarding experience for both students and instructors. Our singing and
youth acting classes also wrapped up the session with a final performance at the Girls Club
House, where families enjoyed seeing the skills and routines the students had been working on.

To help keep families informed, we also introduced a new slideshow during the recitals to
highlight upcoming classes, programs, and community events, helping promote future
opportunities for participants and their families.

Youth Programs:
Our Tiny Twos and Tot Time participants had a wonderful spring session filled with creativity,
learning, and fun. They enjoyed making slime and decorating personalized folder covers to hold
and display all of the work they completed throughout the session. Other favorite activities
included Mother's Day crafts, an egg hunt, a nature walk, chalk and paint play, story time, music
and movement, alphabet activities, and fine motor skill development. The Spring session ended
on a high note with a fun pajama party play day. It was a great way for the children to celebrate
everything they learned while enjoying time with their classmates.

The Lil Chefs program continued to be a success with full classes. Participants enjoyed
preparing both a main dish and dessert while learning kitchen safety, basic cooking skills, and
how to follow recipes. The hands-on experience gave youth the opportunity to build confidence
in the kitchen, work together, and enjoy the meals they created using a variety of cooking
supplies and ingredients.

Senior Center:
The Senior Center continues to provide a vibrant mix of social, recreational, and wellness
opportunities throughout the spring and early summer seasons. Excursions remained one of the
Center's most popular offerings, with numerous trips reaching full capacity. Seniors enjoyed
visits to Valley View Casino, Soboba Casino, Hotel del Coronado, LACMA (Los Angeles County
  Page 5 of 7

  8
 Museum of Art), the Carlsbad Flower Fields, Mariachi USA, Augustine Casino, Santa Barbara
Mission, and additional destinations that encouraged recreation, cultural exploration, and social
connection. The Southeast Senior Committee Senior Ball, held at Commerce Casino with a
Hollywood Glam theme, was another seasonal highlight, with a full bus of participants enjoying
an afternoon of dancing, entertainment, lunch, photo booths, and raffle prizes. Community
interest in the excursion program continues to remain strong, with upcoming trips to Pauma
Casino, the Getty Center, Catalina Island, Morongo Casino, Old Town Temecula, and Solvang's
Danish Days generating significant excitement among participants.
Seasonal celebrations continued to foster meaningful connections within the senior community.
The annual Mother's Day Social, Teatime – Where Love is Always Brewing, welcomed
participants for an afternoon of dancing, tea, sweet treats, raffles, and fellowship, while the
Father's Day celebration, Hats Off to Fathers: Mariachi Fest, featured a live mariachi
performance, folklórico dance performances by senior program participants, root beer cheers,
photo opportunities, goodie bags, raffles, and sombreros. Registration also opened for the
upcoming September senior dance, That's Amore, an Italian-themed celebration where
participants will enjoy lunch, dancing, entertainment, and a festive photo booth.
The Senior Center continues to strengthen its commitment to health, wellness, and social
engagement through a variety of ongoing programs. Participation in mental health workshops
has continued to increase. Chair Yoga has become a valuable addition for participants with
limited mobility, while weekly dance practice, karaoke, and open dancing continue to draw
enthusiastic participation. A new Monday Board Game program has also been introduced,
encouraging seniors to build new friendships through rotating games and social interaction.
Additionally, the Wednesday craft program has experienced tremendous growth, with
participation increasing to the point that craft hours were expanded from two hours to four
hours, allowing participants additional time to share techniques and develop new artistic skills.
The Senior Center also continued to foster valuable community partnerships that enrich the
lives of participants. Through the Phone Lifeline Program, low-income seniors received free
cellular phones and phone service, helping improve digital connectivity and access to essential
resources. Students from KIPP Comienza Community Prep Upper School visited the Center to
perform musical selections for participants, creating a memorable intergenerational experience
that brought seniors and fifth-grade students together through music. Daily nutrition services
also remained a cornerstone of the Center's programming, with HSA continuing to provide hot
lunches Monday through Friday while the Parks & Recreation Department serves
complimentary coffee each day.

Cultural Arts:
Our last exhibition due to budget cuts was Alma Querida, (Dear soul) group art exhibition that
opened on Saturday, April 18 showcasing 63 artists. Along with that we were able to host the
South Gate High School Spring show inside our museum. The excitement from the artists and
families was evident and on full display. Vendors were positioned on the front lawn, artifacts in
museums and an art activity in the gallery.

Our Cultural Arts Coordinator served as a judge for the 2026 Congressional Art Competition an
invite that came from the office of Congresswoman Nanette Barragán.

We hosted more than 200+ LA County Employees for their Wellness Through the Arts initiative.
Participants visited the museum and gallery and conducted a drop-in art activity. STEAM
Legacy High School and South East High School AP Drawing class were also able to host their
exhibitions in the conference room and museum side. It was a great experience having local
youth see their work exhibited out of a classroom setting. We hosted a booth at the Legacy
Wellness fair where students drew images with watercolors. We also provided a Wellness and
  Page 6 of 7

  9
 Emotions mini zine for them to take home and work on.

Cultural Arts collaborated with the Music Center for ¡Dale! Fútbol Watch Party which took place
Friday, June 26. We hosted a jersey manipulation activity for attendees and had an impromptu
fashion show before their Dance DTLA event.

Zine Fiesta 5 was our last event where we hosted two Zine panels, 33 artists/vendors, activities,
piñata and cake to celebrate all our work with the community. It was largest to date since we
had to move vendors outdoors!

  STAFF REPORT ITEM No. 2
To:  Honorable Parks & Recreation Commission
From:  Glenn Massey, Parks Superintendent
Date:  July 29, 2026

Subject:  Review of Grounds & Facility Maintenance 4th Quarter FY 2025/26

Recommended Motion:  Motion to receive and file.

Report Summary:

Grounds Maintenance Activities

  •  We replaced 50 sprinklers at the Southern Avenue Parks.
  •  A three-inch water main break and four broken lateral irrigation lines and 65
  sprinklers at Hollydale Regional Park were repaired this quarter.
  •  Staff raised sunken irrigation valve boxes throughout the Golf Course to prevent
  trip and fall hazards.
  •  This quarter staff have caught over 100 Gophers throughout all City Parks.
  •  Staff are coping with the recent heat waves and syringe cycling the irrigation
  systems to add additional water to all parks to ensure the turf stays green.
  •  Flower beds were mulched and added a few boulders to landscape behind the
  Auditorium as part of our beautification program.

Park Facility Maintenance

Parks Facility Maintenance staff set up and hosted a variety of events; Voting Center at
The Sport Center, Police Trainings, School Culminations, Miss South Gate Pageant,
Rotary Club Mariachi Festival, Earth Day at South Gate Park, Men’s Health Fair, and
Soccer Watch Parties, ongoing Red Cross Blood Drives, and LA County food give
aways just to mention a few.

Due to the high use of SG Park, Staff continues to do a third daily inspection and
cleaning, in the late afternoon to our outdoor restrooms. We remain vigilant when
addressing the ongoing challenges with restroom cleanliness with a routine restroom
disinfecting program. This includes the use of the C3 Machine to apply disinfectants and
cleaners. Once the product is sprayed, staff scrubs floors, walls, and fixtures to insure
sanitary conditions.
  Page 1 of 2

  11
 We have continued the use of Electrostatic Disinfecting Equipment for more coverage in
our cleaning and disinfecting efforts for both indoor and outdoor restroom facilities,
along with a pressure washing program. These disinfecting and cleaning tools are used
consistently. Set-ups for all events require us to disinfect all tables, chairs, door
handles, and A/V equipment.

To accommodate classes, reservations, and events, staff schedules have been
adjusted to ensure full coverage and support. Facility staff have displayed exceptional
flexibility and professionalism in managing the transition between regular operations
and new demands, consistently responding to the evolving needs of the Division.

The Community Service Worker program is ongoing; we are still limiting the intake to 15
people maximum per day.

Parks are busy with many events, classes, picnics, and sports activities. Both Grounds
Maintenance and Facility Maintenance staff work together to make sure all events run
smoothly.

  August 13, 2026
  STAFF REPORT ITEM No. 3
To:  Honorable Parks & Recreation Commission
From:  Tina De La Rosa, Director of Parks & Recreation
Date:  July 30, 2026

Subject:  Update on Parks & Recreation Department Major Projects

Recommended Motion:  Motion to receive and file.

Report Summary: The Parks & Recreation Department maintains more than 185
acres of parkland, along with numerous community centers, recreational facilities, and
support buildings throughout the city. To ensure these amenities remain safe,
functional, and enjoyable for the community, the Department continually performs
routine maintenance and capital improvement projects to enhance our parks and
facilities.
The following is an update on several recently completed capital improvement projects
and the remaining work associated with each project.

Auditorium Roof Project
The South Gate Park Auditorium Roof Replacement Project was successfully
completed in April 2026. The new roof has resolved the long-standing leak issues that
have affected the facility for several years. Completion of this project protects one of the
City's most utilized community facilities and extends the life of the building for years to
come.
Estimated cost:  $1.2 million
Current Cost:  $1 million

Circle Park
The Circle Park Renovation Project was completed, and the city celebrated its Grand
Opening on October 13, 2025. The renovated park includes new picnic areas,
basketball courts, a futsal court, pickleball court, playground improvements, and other
amenities that have become a valued recreational destination for the community.
As part of the project's warranty period, several items require corrective work and are
currently being addressed by the contractor:
  • The pickleball court developed surface cracks and is currently being renovated.
  • The basketball court has experienced minor surface cracking and will be
  repainted following completion of the pickleball court repairs.
  Page 1 of 3
  13
   •  The futsal court has a drainage design issue that allows water to collect during
  rain events. A French drain will be installed to improve drainage and mitigate
  future flooding.
The Department continues to work closely with the contractor to ensure all warranty
items are completed in accordance with project specifications.
Estimated cost:  $7 million
Current funding:  $7 million

Scoreboard Replacement Project
The Sports Center Gymnasium Scoreboard Enhancement Project was completed in
March 2026. The project significantly modernized the facility by installing professional-
style scoreboards throughout the gymnasium.
Improvements include:
  • Two additional scoreboards are installed for Courts A and B, bringing the total
  number of scoreboards to six.
  • Installation of shot clocks for competitive play.
  • LED backboard perimeter lighting to enhance game operations.
  • Customized scoreboards featuring the City of South Gate logo.
These improvements provide a professional game-day experience for youth sports,
tournaments, and community events hosted at the Sports Center.
Estimated cost:  $85,000
Current Cost :  $78,000

Swim Stadium Scoreboard Replacement Project
The new Swim Stadium scoreboard was installed in June 2026. The new LED display
provides exceptional visibility for swimmers, officials, and spectators and is a significant
upgrade from the previous scoreboard.
The final phase of the project includes installation of the electronic touchpad timing
system, which is expected to be completed soon. Once installed, the facility will be fully
equipped to support competitive swim meets with modern timing technology.
Estimated cost:  $85,000
Current cost:  $174,000

Gardendale Tot Lot Surfacing Project
The Gardendale Tot Lot Rubberized Surfacing Project was completed in May 2026. The
existing sand surfacing was replaced with poured-in-place rubberized safety surfacing
through Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) funding.
The new surface enhances accessibility, improves safety for children, reduces ongoing
maintenance, and provides a more inclusive play environment for families visiting
Gardendale Park.
Estimated cost:  $120,000
Current cost:  $245,000

Transit Charging Station
The City's Transit Division, which operates the GATE Bus system, is preparing to
transition its fleet to electric vehicles in accordance with California's transit regulations
and zero-emission vehicle requirements. To support this transition, the city must first
develop the necessary charging infrastructure.
  Page 2 of 3
  14
 The proposed project includes the construction of a new electric bus charging station at
South Gate Park. The facility will provide the infrastructure needed to charge and
support the City's future electric bus fleet, ensuring reliable transit service while meeting
state environmental mandates.
The project is currently in the planning and design phase, and staff is working to finalize
the project scope and cost estimates. A substantial portion of the project funding is
anticipated to come from grant funding through Southern California Edison (SCE),
which will help offset the overall project costs.
  • Estimated Cost: To Be Determined
  • Current Funding: Grant funding through Southern California Edison (SCE)
  (pending final award and project budget)

  Page 3 of 3
  15
